description:
Hello,I'm Kishore Kumar Manikandan,an Ex-AI/ML Engineer and BTU Cottbus Cyber Security Master's student.

Project C.O.S.M.I.C. AEGIS an offline, camera-based AI medical guardian for astronauts in deep space. I have the core AI and security architecture covered, but I need an awesome crew to bring it to life:

Frontend/UI Devs: To build a sleek mission control dashboard.

Hardware Hackers: To integrate camera feeds and edge devices.

Medical Enthusiasts: To structure space medicine protocols.
summary:
C.O.S.M.I.C. AEGIS (Cottbus Orbital Software for Medical Informatics & Care) is an AI-powered, camera-only health-monitoring system designed for autonomous astronaut healthcare during deep-space missions, operating entirely offline without internet connectivity.

Astronauts face critical physiological and psychological challenges while enduring severe communication delays with Earth. C.O.S.M.I.C. AEGIS leverages existing spacecraft cabin cameras and onboard AI—combining YOLO and Detectron2 for precise exercise posture tracking, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for analyzing visual health indicators, and a local Large Language Model (LLM) to deliver instant, protocol-based medical guidance. A centralized command dashboard tracks longitudinal trends, while SHA-256 hash-chained logs ensure tamper-evident record keeping. Operating within an average latency of 1.5 seconds, the system requires no invasive wearables or external sensors.

By transforming standard cabin feeds into proactive, offline medical intelligence, C.O.S.M.I.C. AEGIS empowers astronauts to monitor health metrics, manage fatigue, and navigate medical protocols independently. This solution bridges the gap between deep-space isolation and immediate healthcare access, safeguarding crews on the International Space Station, Lunar Gateway, and future Mars expeditions.
details:
• What it does and how it works

C.O.S.M.I.C. AEGIS is a browser-based health monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions. It is a single web app, live at https://cosmic-aegis-beryl.vercel.app, with no install or hardware needed. It opens on a dashboard with a 30-second animated, narrated story for new visitors. The story covers the problem, why it matters, our idea, what we built, and the limits of the prototype.

  1. Daily check-in (mental health). The astronaut logs mood, stress, sleep hours and fatigue. The app tracks 7-day averages. It raises a gentle alert if 3 or more of the last 5 check-ins report high stress, or if average sleep falls below 6.5 hours.
  2. Muscle and bone. The astronaut logs exercise sessions (type, minutes, strength). The app shows days active in the last 7, minutes trained, and strength trend compared with earlier sessions. Because microgravity causes muscle and bone loss, a drop in consistency or strength raises a flag. Bone status here is derived from activity consistency only. It is not a bone measurement.
  3. Cardiovascular. The astronaut logs heart rate, blood pressure and SpO2. The app compares the latest values with illustrative ranges, shows 7-day changes, and charts the trend.
  4. Dashboard. It combines the three areas into one overall score from 0 to 100, with Nominal, Watch and Review status colours and a prioritised alert list.
    • an animated astronaut companion with a calming breathing pacer (4-7-8) and a reaction-time test;
    • a hex byte viewer;
    • a module checklist;
    • a mock ground-control view with a simulated one-way signal delay of about 9.7 minutes;
    • a delay-tolerant message queue that holds messages until the “link” returns.
  5. SOS practice. A 10-second countdown ring with a siren tone. It is for rehearsal only, and nothing is sent anywhere.
  6. AEGIS assistant (chat and voice). A floating assistant reads the user’s own entries and explains them in plain language: how they are doing, why stress is flagged, sleep tips, and what their heart readings show. A “Read my guidance aloud” button speaks a personalised, step-by-step plan through the browser’s speech engine. The plan covers stress, sleep, heart, and muscle and bone, and ends with a safety reminder. The assistant is a scripted, rule-based helper, not an AI model.
  7. Sources page. It lists which parts are real and which are simulated, plus the NASA references we used.

All data is simulated and stays in the user’s browser (localStorage). A reset button restores the sample data.

Benefits

  • Gives crew early, easy-to-read awareness of slow changes in mood, sleep, fitness and vitals.
  • Helps prepare clear, organised information for the crew medical officer or ground team.
  • Supports autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed by minutes.
  • Calming tools and spoken guidance support psychological wellbeing in isolation.
  • Needs no wearables or special equipment, so it is cheap and easy to try.

Intended impact

We want crews to notice problems earlier and feel less alone, and to make routine self-monitoring something they actually keep doing. It is awareness only. It does not diagnose, predict or treat, and it is not a medical device. Our longer-term vision is to connect real wearable or habitat sensor data and a safe language-model assistant. Those would run under medical oversight and a real data-privacy review.

Tools and technology

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, React Router 7
  • Styling and charts: Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts, lucide-react icons, Google Fonts (Orbitron, Rajdhani, Space Mono)
  • Browser APIs: Web Speech API (voice), Web Audio (tones and alarms), Canvas (animated starfield), localStorage (data)
  • Hosting and workflow: GitHub for version control, Vercel for automatic deployment
  • Testing: headless Edge screenshots for visual checks, and desktop and mobile checks in the browser
  • Hardware: none beyond a normal browser
  • AI assistance: used for code and visuals, and disclosed on the site
  • Reference material: the NASA Human Research Program pages and evidence reports listed in the NASA Data section

Creativity

  • A mission-control look with a simulated live ticker (heart rate, oxygen, CO2, cabin temperature, radiation).
  • A 30-second self-playing story on the landing page.
  • Voice guidance generated from the user’s own entries, not a fixed script.
  • A friendly astronaut companion instead of a clinical form.
  • SOS practice and a delay-tolerant queue that make signal delay something you can feel.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: every value is labelled simulated. The site states it is not a medical device and not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. No real NASA dataset is loaded, and the NASA documents were used as design references.
  • Safety: crisis or emergency wording gets a redirect to real help, never a scripted answer. The assistant never diagnoses.
  • Privacy: no accounts, no server and no tracking. Data stays on the device.
  • Accessibility: story captions are always on, narration is optional, reduced-motion is respected, and the controls work with a keyboard. Status is shown with text as well as colour.
  • Connectivity: the delay-tolerant design assumes the Earth link is slow or intermittent.
  • Scope: we built a working prototype across three health areas rather than a broad but shallow one.
  • Future path: the scripted assistant and the simulated inputs are isolated, so a real model or real sensors can replace them later.
